title: Burst crediting pricing — raw notes
content:
Quick brain dump: burst crediting model for smoothing spikes + simple UX for PAYG customers. Not polished — working thoughts for product + finance sync.

Context and goal:
- Many small teams driven by usage spikes (demo days, campaigns) hate strictly linear per-token pricing because tail spikes blow budget and cause support tickets.
- Want lightweight credit bucket that: absorbs short spikes, incentivizes pre-commit for predictable heavy usage, and is easy to reason about for devs.
- Keep compliance and accounting simple (credits map to tokens or token-equivalents).

Assumptions (ballpark for back-of-envelope):
- Average model mix: 60% Llama-13B-like (chat/generation), 30% Llama-7B-like (smaller gen + chat), 10% embedding/short calls.
- Average tokens per generation request: 1,250 tokens (prompt + completion).
- Embeddings counted as 1 unit per 512 tokens for equivalence.
- Unit cost (infra/e2e) to Redwood per token: assume $0.0000025/token (i.e., $2.5 per million tokens) — this is raw infra + amortized infra ops + networking.
- Desired gross margin target (hosted): 75% on PAYG; for committed/reserved offers target margin may be lower.

Simple math primitives:
- cost_per_token = $0.0000025
- target_price_payg = cost_per_token / (1 - margin) => with 75% margin price = 0.0000025 / 0.25 = $0.00001/token (=$10 per million)
- translate to credits: 1 credit ~= 1 token for UX simplicity OR 1 credit ~= 100 tokens to keep numbers small.
  - Prefer 1 credit = 100 tokens (so customer sees tens/hundreds of credits rather than millions).

If 1 credit = 100 tokens:
- cost_per_credit = 100 * 0.0000025 = $0.00025
- price_per_credit (75% margin) = $0.001 (0.1 cents)
- So PAYG price ~ $0.001/credit => $10 per million tokens as above.

Bursting behavior idea:
- Each account has a monthly bucket of credits (earned via pay-as-you-go top-up or subscription).
- Allow overdraft: temporary negative credit balance up to a cap (e.g., -2x monthly baseline) that triggers higher marginal price or throttling.
- Refill point: at monthly invoice cycle credits reset/are replenished. Unused credits could expire after 3 months (or optionally roll over a small fraction).

Mechanics (sketch):
- Starter: free trial 5,000 credits (500k tokens) to test.
- PAYG top-up: buy credits at posted price (no commitment).
- Monthly subscription tiers (prepay):
  - Growth (monthly): 100k credits = 10M tokens priced at 85% of PAYG credit price (i.e., small discount).
  - Scale (monthly): 1M credits = 100M tokens priced at 70% of PAYG credit price.
  - Enterprise: custom (reserved capacity + credits + SLA).
- Overdraft protection: while on Growth/Scale, allow burst to -50% of monthly credits for up to 72 hours; fee for overdraft = 2x per-credit price for overdraft tokens (deters abuse but allows real spikes).

Unit economics examples (toy scenarios):
- Small app (demo week): 200k tokens/day for 7 days = 1.4M tokens. If paying PAYG at $10/million => $14 total. If used within Starter trial might be free; if spikes beyond trial, top-up is cheap but surprising.
- Fast-growing SaaS: 50M tokens/mo ~ price = 50 * $10 = $500. If on Scale (30% discount): $350/mo. Cost to Redwood: 50M * 0.0000025 = $125. Gross margin (Scale) = (350 - 125)/350 = 64% (below target but acceptable for committed revenue).

Why credit abstraction helps:
- UX: credits are visible in Console as single number; easier for product PMs to set alerts.
- Spikes: overdraft allows non-blocking bursts with a visible surcharge — reduces emergency support.
- Bundling: credits can be bundled with observability retention or support add-ons.

Potential pitfalls / attack vectors:
- Arbitrage between credits and PAYG if discounts too deep (customers buy credits at scale just to resell? improbable but need guardrails).
- Complex mapping for mixed workloads (embeddings vs long generations) — keep equivalence simple and transparent.
- Accounting headaches if credits roll over long periods or are refundable.

Open product questions:
- Should credits be token-equivalent or compute-equivalent (i.e., weight by model type/length)? Simpler to be token-equivalent but may subsidize very heavy models.
- Overdraft cap: flat multiplier (x1.5 or x2) or absolute credit amount? Flat multiplier easier.
- Rollover policy: none vs small rollover (5-10%) — rollover increases deferred liability.
- UI/UX: show "burn rate" estimate and projected runout time (tokens/day -> credits/day).

Simple experiment to validate assumptions (A/B):
- Create two cohorts of new signups for 30 days:
  - Cohort A: pure PAYG price shown
  - Cohort B: credit bucket UX with small free trial and overdraft allowed (2x cap)
- Track: conversion to paid, average monthly spend, incidence of overdraft, support tickets.
- Key metric: % of accounts that convert to monthly commit within 60 days and LTV/3mo payback.

Operational notes for finance + engineering:
- Billing: credits consumed at request completion time; streaming tokens incrementally decrement credits in real-time to prevent overspend.
- Metering: need model routing tags and token counters per-request; embeddings normalized to credit-equivalents in meter pipeline.
- Alerts: set beta accounts to threshold alerts at 25% and 5% remaining credits.

To-dos (next steps):
- Run a micro-sensitivity calc in spreadsheet with variable cost_per_token (0.0000015–0.000004) and multiple discount breakpoints; estimate margin for each tier. (owner: Arjun)
- Prototype console UX for credits and overdraft. (owner: Samira)
